BREAK-EVEN
Variant (b) is cheaper than same-container 2 vCPU / 4 GiB whenever browser time plus grace is under 100% of agent running time. Against 1 vCPU / 4 GiB, it is cheaper below 50%. On top of that, variant (b) costs about 10 extra person-days and adds latency.

ONE-OFF ENGINEERING
- About 59 person-days base + 15 contingency ≈ 74 person-days, about 3.5 person-months.
- Phase 1 (agents can browse, no live view): about 32 person-days.
- Phase 2 (live view + takeover, apps): about 27 person-days.

CONTEXT ONLY, not part of this option: AgentBay
- Assumes a 2 vCPU / 4 GiB session at the domestic price (¥0.44/h, an unverified spec) plus the Pro plan floor of ¥999/month.

- Light case, 1000 DAU: about ¥5,399/month. Our cost here is ¥3,318–8,066.

options.ux:
WHAT THE USER SEES

- Turning it on. Each agent gets a "浏览器" (browser) switch. Turning it on rebuilds the sandbox at the bigger size through the existing version-rebuild path, which takes seconds to tens of seconds (unmeasured). The plan editor gets a "可以用浏览器上网" (may browse the web) pre-authorization. Without it, Claude and Codex ask for approval on every click, which is unusable.

- While the agent browses. The chat shows tool steps as today ("打开 …", "点击 …", i.e. "opening …", "clicking …"). Playwright MCP reads pages from the accessibility tree, so most steps are text, not screenshots. Screenshots go to the agent. They cannot ride the event stream (16 KiB string cap), so the user sees them only through `browser_share` (saved as an artifact) or the live view. A "查看浏览器" (view browser) button opens the live view.

- Live view. A JPEG stream from Page.startScreencast, about 2–10 fps while the page changes and nothing while it is static. Expected lag is a few hundred ms: mainland phone ↔ Tokyo server ↔ sandbox [assumption, unmeasured]. It uses about 9 MB/min of mobile data at 3 fps, so warn on cellular. It feels like a slightly laggy remote desktop. Fine for watching and for typing a password. Clumsy for slider CAPTCHAs, which also tend to flag synthetic drags.

- Takeover for logins and CAPTCHAs. The agent calls browser_handoff ("需要你登录小红书", "please log in to Xiaohongshu"). The phone gets a push. The user taps it, the live view opens in control mode with a text bar for Chinese IME and keys (Enter, Backspace, Tab), the user does the step and taps 完成 (Done), and the agent continues. If nobody responds within 30 min, the agent is told and the run carries on or fails. The user can also tap "接管" (take over) at any time. That interrupts the agent's current turn first.

- Saved logins. Cookies stay in the profile inside the workspace. They survive pause (the browser is frozen) and archive (the profile is encrypted in OSS). After an archive, the next wake restarts Chromium from disk; the user stays logged in unless the site expired the session or its risk control reacts to the new session. "清除浏览器数据" (clear browser data) wipes the profile.

- Which sites work. Every site sees a Tokyo datacenter IP.
  - Foreign sites, docs and SaaS: usually fine, and Google/GitHub are reachable. This is also a compliance issue; see security.
  - Xiaohongshu, Weibo and Douyin show the user's posts with an "IP属地 日本" (IP location: Japan) label.
  - Taobao, WeChat web and banks are likely to block or keep challenging (anecdotal reports). For those, the right path is the user's own computer (computer_* / WBS 14.4), not this browser.

- Speed. Chromium starts in about 1–2 s once the sandbox runs (unmeasured). Waking an archived instance adds the workspace restore, and the profile adds roughly 50–300 MB to it [assumption]. JS-heavy Chinese sites are slower from Tokyo, and slow on 1 vCPU. 2 vCPU is noticeably better [assumption].
options.security_compliance:
SECURITY
- Trust boundary. The pod is the boundary: one sandbox per instance per user, and ACS pods are isolated from each other. Inside it, the untrusted agent has full CDP access to its own browser. That means it can read every cookie of every site the user logged into in that instance (Network.getAllCookies). It can see anything typed during a takeover, passwords included. It can act as the user on those sites. Playwright MCP's core tools include browser_evaluate, browser_run_code_unsafe ("RCE-equivalent") and browser_file_upload. None of this escalates beyond the shell the agent already has, but a prompt injection from a web page can steer the agent into misusing the user's logged-in sessions or sending workspace files to a site. Variants (a) and (b) do not change this while the agent holds CDP.
- Mitigations:
  - The egress proxy is the real control point: private ranges and metadata blocked, ports 80/443 only, per-instance byte and connection caps, logs, kill switch, optional per-plan allowlist.
  - Browser-level allowlists (Playwright --allowed-origins, OpenClaw ssrfPolicy) are documented as not being security boundaries.
  - Payments and banking should not be marketed. browser_handoff is for the human step, and high-risk actions keep needing approval. Approvals use ACP kinds, which express intent only, not a boundary.
  - Encourage a separate instance for sensitive logins, and make "clear browser data" easy.
- Chromium hardening:
  - --no-sandbox is likely needed, because ACS rejects privileged pods and privilege escalation; user-namespace support is unverified. A renderer exploit then runs as uid 1001 in the pod, which the agent already is.
  - Keep CDP on 127.0.0.1 only. Live view goes through the authenticated envd exec path, never an exposed port.
  - --disable-background-networking stops calls to Google.
  - Weekly Chrome security releases mean template rebuilds every week or two. Debian's chromium can lag upstream.
- Data at rest:
  - The profile is archived inside the workspace tar, encrypted per user (AES-256-GCM with the user's DEK). Account deletion drops the DEK, so archives become unreadable.
  - Whether ACS ephemeral storage is encrypted while the pod runs or is paused is not documented.
  - Caches go to /tmp and are excluded from the archive.
  - Proxy logs (host, bytes, instance) are personal data: set a retention period. 网络安全法 (Cybersecurity Law) log-retention duties should be checked with counsel.

COMPLIANCE (needs legal advice; not settled here)
- Cross-border. The Tokyo deployment already stores mainland users' workspaces abroad. Cookies, logins and browsing history add sensitive personal information, so PIPL Art. 38/39 applies: standard contract or another mechanism, plus separate consent. The privacy text must name the cookie/profile storage and the Japan egress IP.
- Circumvention risk. A Tokyo browser whose screen is streamed to phones in mainland China can reach sites blocked there (Google, YouTube, X…). Regulators could see this as providing a cross-border access service (MIIT 2017 notice 信管函〔2017〕32号), and Alibaba Cloud's terms forbid illegal proxy use. Options to discuss with counsel: deny blocked-site categories at the proxy, or restrict live view to handoff moments. This risk applies equally to any overseas cloud browser, AgentBay Singapore included.
- Automated access. 网络数据安全管理条例 (Network Data Security Regulations) Art. 18 requires that automated collection not disrupt the target service. Use per-instance rate limits, and ToS rules against 刷单/刷榜 (order-brushing and ranking manipulation), spam and scraping abuse.
- No ICP filing is needed for a Tokyo host.
- Licences: Chromium (BSD-3 plus third-party licences), Playwright and Playwright MCP (Apache-2.0), fonts-noto-cjk (OFL-1.1) are fine for hosting. Avoid Browserless (SSPL §13) and AGPL tools (nodriver, Lightpanda). If chrome-devtools-mcp is ever used, turn off --usageStatistics and --performanceCrux, or users' URLs go to Google.
risks: The egress proxy (WBS 2.7) is the critical path and the security-critical piece. It is not built, and even today's 'no internet' ACS baseline has not been verified on the real Tokyo cluster (docs/sandbox-acs.md §8).

Sizing has not been measured. If Chromium plus the agent needs 2 vCPU / 4 GiB, a browser-enabled sandbox costs twice today's (¥0.49/h vs ¥0.25/h). The ACS traffic-proxy sidecar (0.2 vCPU / 128 MB) may round specs up by about 25% more. Whether the agent-sandbox class follows the general-purpose spec table is undocumented.

Tokyo datacenter IP: Chinese platforms label posts 'IP属地 日本' (IP location: Japan). Taobao, WeChat web and banks are likely to block or keep challenging. Datacenter IPs are the main bot signal. CAPTCHA and anti-bot work is an arms race we should not promise to win.

Compliance (needs legal advice): a Tokyo browser streamed to mainland phones can reach blocked sites, which could be seen as an unapproved cross-border access service (MIIT 2017 notice; Alibaba Cloud terms). Cookies and browsing history leaving China fall under PIPL Art. 38/39.

A prompt-injected agent holds raw CDP. It can steal the session cookies of every site logged into that instance, read passwords typed during takeover, and upload workspace files. The only hard controls are the per-instance sandbox and the egress proxy.

Live view relies on envd exec streams through sandbox-manager. Throughput, latency, base64 overhead and the 600 s idle timeout have not been tested. If it is too slow, the fallback (routing /kruise/<id>/<port> for another port) is also untested.

Chromium inside ACS: its own sandbox probably cannot start (ACS rejects privileged pods and privilege escalation; user-namespace support is unverified), so --no-sandbox is likely; /dev/shm is 64 MiB by default.
Chrome ships security fixes weekly. Browser templates need frequent rebuilds and rollouts through archive/restore, and Debian's chromium can lag upstream.
Profile persistence: cookies (SQLite) can be lost if tar runs while Chromium writes; stale Singleton locks can block relaunch; caches can bloat archives toward the 4 GiB cap and slow every wake.

Agent integration is uneven. Platform tools, and so browser_handoff, reach only Claude, Codex and Hermes today. Pi's MCP under rpc mode and OpenClaw's attachOnly browser in ACP sessions are unverified. Without tool-name pre-authorization, Claude and Codex ask for approval on every MCP call.
Upstream churn: Playwright MCP is pre-1.0 (0.0.83). Hermes after 0.19 replaces its browser tools. OpenClaw's bundled browser plugin may start its own Chromium unless configured off.

Variant (b) networking does not fit ACS: allowOut is fixed per IP, and a CIDR rule would open traffic between tenants, so CDP must be relayed through the server. Variant (a) depends on multi-container pods and emptyDir working with the agent-sandbox class and pause/resume, which is unverified; Cube cannot run it.
Effort: about 74 person-days including contingency, about half of it the live view, takeover and two native app UIs. A team busy with launch work may not have that capacity.
strengths: Runs in Tokyo next to the agent, inside the existing one-sandbox-per-instance isolation. No new vendor, no region or account mismatch (AgentBay has no Tokyo region and a domestic key works only in the mainland), and no ¥999/month Pro floor.

Egress stays fully under our policy. The same proxy carries out WBS 2.7, which is needed before launch anyway, and later gives all agents controlled web access. The sandbox still has no direct internet and no NAT is added.
Saved logins come almost for free: the profile sits in the workspace and rides the existing per-user DEK-encrypted OSS archive and crypto-shred on deletion.

One CDP endpoint serves all five agents through one MCP server, Playwright MCP. Its endpoint can later be swapped for a mainland browser pool or AgentBay/AgentRun without changing what the agents see.

Live view and takeover need no new public port: frames go through the existing authenticated envd exec path and gateway WebSocket. The design mirrors AgentBay's call-for-user flow under our own control.

Low extra compute: about ¥3.7–7.4 per DAU per month (1 or 2 vCPU / 4 GiB at 60 agent-min/day). Downloaded page traffic is inbound and free on Alibaba Cloud; only live-view frames cost about ¥0.5 per DAU per month.
Everything is permissively licensed open source (Chromium, Playwright, Playwright MCP, Noto CJK), which is fine for a hosted service.
It can be built in phases: phase 1 (agents can browse, about 32 person-days) is useful before phase 2 (live view and takeover, about 27 person-days).

options.name: BUY: Alibaba Cloud Wuying AgentBay cloud browser, run by our Tokyo server as browser_* platform tools
options.architecture:
Shape: our Tokyo server is the only thing that talks to AgentBay. It does so through a new group of platform tools (browser_*). AgentBay is not a sandbox backend, and the agent sandbox does not change.

1) ACCOUNT AND REGION (the first decision)
- What I checked on 2026-10-29:
  - SDK 0.22.3 knows only cn-hangzhou (the default), ap-southeast-1 and us-east-1 (agentbay/_common/config.py:19,26). The endpoint pattern is agentbay.<region>.aliyuncs.com.
  - DNS (dns.alidns.com DoH) returns NXDOMAIN for agentbay.ap-northeast-1.aliyuncs.com and agentbay.cn-hongkong.aliyuncs.com.
  - The three known endpoints resolve. Each answered an unsigned probe with HTTP 400 MissingTimestamp.
  - So there is no Tokyo AgentBay.
- API keys only work in their own region (SDK docs):
  - Our existing domestic (aliyun.com) account can use Hangzhou only.
  - Singapore or Virginia needs a separate international account. Our earlier international account got stuck at real-name verification (docs/deploy-aliyun-sg.md, section 8 table).
- Option D (my default): domestic account, browsers in Hangzhou, called cross-border from Tokyo.
  - Same account and bill as today. The cheapest per hour.
  - Browsing most likely leaves from a mainland IP (inferred), which suits Chinese sites.
  - Google, YouTube, Wikipedia, X and ChatGPT are unreachable, and GitHub only partly.
- Option I: international account, browsers in Singapore.
  - Foreign sites work.
  - Chinese sites see a 新加坡 (Singapore) IP location and are likely to trigger risk controls.
  - Users' cookies are stored abroad.
- Running both doubles the plan fee and splits saved logins by region. Not for v1.

2) NEW COMPONENTS
- crates/agentbay: a Rust client for the WuyingAI OpenAPI.
  - It is RPC style, version 2025-05-06, sent as a form POST. Auth is "Anonymous", with the key sent as the form field Authorization=Bearer <key>. I verified this in the SDK (api/client.py: CreateMcpSession around line 255, GetCdpLink around line 2768; _async/browser.py get_endpoint_url).
  - Calls we need: CreateMcpSession (fields include ImageId, ContextId, PersistenceDataList, Labels, Timeout, MaxRuntime, ManualRelease, EnableRecord, ExternalUserId), InitBrowser, GetCdpLink, GetSession (returns ResourceUrl and WsUrl), RefreshSessionIdleTime, ReleaseMcpSession/DeleteSessionAsync, ListSession (by labels), and GetContext/ListContexts/DeleteContext/SyncContext.
  - There is no Rust SDK. I could not confirm a public API reference (the api.aliyun.com page is rendered by JavaScript), so the generated Python SDK is the de facto spec.
- crates/browser: a CDP driver, built on chromiumoxide or a thin client on tokio-tungstenite (already in Cargo.lock).
  - It provides an accessibility snapshot with element refs, click/type/press/scroll/select, Input.insertText for Chinese text, tabs and dialogs, and JPEG screenshots up to 1568 px on the long edge.
  - It can be reused later for WBS 14.4 (desktop browser via chromiumoxide).
- crates/proto/src/browser.rs: the tool catalog, modelled on proto::computer (names, JSON schemas, risk tier, timeouts).
- crates/orchestrator/src/browser.rs: BrowserTools implements PlatformTools (shim.rs:97-102) and contains the session manager. It joins the ToolSet built in crates/server/src/workers.rs:131-157.
- Store, new migration 0031:
  - browser_contexts: instance → AgentBay context id and region.
  - browser_sessions: at most one active row per instance.
- Gateway: crates/gateway/src/routes/browser.rs, covering live view, "takeover done" and "forget logins".

3) ONE TOOL CALL, END TO END
- Path: the agent calls mcp__thinktin__browser_open → agent-shim mcp-bridge → platform_tool_call → executor → BrowserTools.call(ctx).
- The session manager takes user, instance and run only from ToolContext, never from the tool's arguments. This is the same rule as computer routing (orchestrator/src/computer.rs:1-6).
- If the instance has no live session, it starts one:
  - GetContext("thk-<instance uuid>", create).
  - CreateMcpSession with ImageId=browser_latest, the context with auto-upload, Labels {env, user uuid, instance uuid, run uuid}, 5-minute idle release, a capped MaxRuntime and EnableRecord=false.
  - InitBrowser(BrowserOption: viewport, solve_captchas, call_for_user, optional use_stealth and proxies).
  - GetCdpLink. The worker then opens the CDP WebSocket. The documented example host is wss://gw-cn-hangzhou-ai-linux.wuyinggw.com:8008.
- The result goes back as MCP content (a text snapshot plus a JPEG image block) via PlatformToolResult.
- Platform tool results are not written as events (executor.rs:1849-1865), so screenshots never hit the 16 KiB event cap. The app sees only the tool-call titles.
- At turn end, run end, cancel or any wait state, the session is released with a context sync (cookies and localStorage are uploaded).
- A sweeper in workers.rs lists our sessions by the env label and kills any that has no live run. Idle sessions are billed, so this matters.

4) SANDBOX AND EGRESS
- Nothing changes in the sandbox: no Chromium in deploy/templates/Dockerfile and no allowOut change. The CDP URL and the API key never enter the sandbox.
- So browsing does NOT wait for the egress proxy (WBS 2.7).
- The browser's own traffic leaves through AgentBay's network, and we cannot filter it: the domain allowlist is Windows-only, and *.aliyuncs.com is always allowed.
- It also has no route into our VPC (inferred: no public IP, and we configure no VPC).

5) WHY THE AGENT DOES NOT GET THE CDP URL
- The CDP URL is a bearer link: anyone holding it controls a browser that carries the user's cookies. A prompt-injected agent could navigate somewhere with the URL in it and leak it.
- Handing it over would also need a new allowOut domain and per-agent wiring (OpenClaw cdpUrl, Hermes BROWSER_CDP_URL, playwright-mcp for the others).
- I keep this only as a later option for OpenClaw's and Hermes's native browser tools.

6) LIVE VIEW AND TAKEOVER
- Live view: the app calls the gateway. The gateway checks ownership and gets a fresh ResourceUrl via GetSession. If no session is live, it first creates a "takeover session" on the instance's context. The app opens the URL in a WebView.
- Takeover reuses the vault_request pattern (orchestrator/src/vault.rs:1-5; gateway/src/routes/vault.rs:315,407):
  - browser_ask_user records a request, sends a push and ends the turn.
  - The browser session is released, so nothing is billed while we wait.
  - The user opens the live view and logs in, then taps Done.
  - That releases the session with a context sync and starts a follow-up run.
- AgentBay's own call_for_user can feed the same flow. It sends codes 101 captcha, 102 login and 103 pay with max_wait_time 180 s over the session WsUrl, and takeover-done goes back to target "wuying_cdp_mcp_server". But 180 s is too short for a reply driven by a push notification, so it is optional.

7) APPROVALS AND WHICH AGENTS GET IT
- Risk tiers:
  - Read-only: snapshot, screenshot, tabs.
  - Normal: open, click, type, press, scroll.
- Both tiers can be pre-authorized with one plan-policy switch, "may browse the web".
- Without that switch, Claude and Codex ask for approval before every MCP call (docs/agent-integration.md section 5), which makes browsing unusable.
- Platform tools reach only Claude, Codex and Hermes. OpenClaw and Pi need MCP injection through agent-shim config.rs first (an optional work item).

options.cost_model:
PRICES USED (from the survey; AgentBay billing pages)
- Domestic: CPU ¥0.12/core·h, memory ¥0.05/GB·h, billed per second. Pro ¥999/month (200 concurrent, 1 TiB storage). Ultra ¥1,499/month, plus ¥10 per extra concurrent session per month.
- International: CPU $0.027/core·h, memory $0.0113/GB·h. Pro $149/month.
- The CDP endpoint is not available on the free Basic plan, so Pro is the minimum for agent control over CDP.
- Idle running sessions are billed.

ASSUMPTIONS (all mine, none verified)
- A1: a browser_latest session is 2 vCPU / 4 GiB. Its spec is not published; 2c4g is the default spec for custom images.
- A2: 30 active browser minutes per daily active user (DAU) per day. Sensitivity runs use 10 and 60.
- A3: billed time is 1.15 × active time (create/init, idle tail before release, takeover sessions).
- A4: 30 days per month.
- A5: peak concurrency is 3 × the average over a 12-hour (720-minute) active day.
- A6: basic bandwidth is enough (no premium bandwidth at ¥0.8/GB).
- A7: at most 200 MB of context per instance, which fits inside Pro's 1 TiB.
- A8: ¥7.1 per USD, used only for one comparison.

UNIT PRICE PER SESSION-HOUR
- Domestic: 2×0.12 + 4×0.05 = ¥0.44/h.
- International: 2×0.027 + 4×0.0113 = $0.0992/h.

DOMESTIC (Hangzhou), billed hours = DAU × 30 min × 30 days ÷ 60 × 1.15

| DAU | Billed hours/month | Compute | + Pro | Total/month | Per DAU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 (today's test) | 172.5 | ¥75.9 | ¥999 | ¥1,075 | ¥107.5 |
| 100 | 1,725 | ¥759 | ¥999 | ¥1,758 | ¥17.6 |
| 1000 | 17,250 | ¥7,590 | ¥999 | ¥8,589 | ¥8.6 |

- 10 DAU: the ¥999 plan fee is 93% of the cost. It is more than twice the whole current launch budget of ¥390–450/month (docs/deploy-aliyun-sg.md 8.9).
- 100 DAU: average concurrency is 100×30×1.15/720 = 4.8, so the peak is about 14, which is already above Basic's limit of 10.

Sensitivity at 1000 DAU:

- 60 min/day: 34,500 h × 0.44 = ¥15,180. Peak concurrency is 95.8 × 3 ≈ 288, which is over 200, so we need Ultra: ¥1,499 + 88 × ¥10 = ¥2,379. Total ¥17,559.
- If the browser spec is really 4c8g: the unit price doubles to ¥0.88/h.
- The domestic billing example uses CPU at ¥0.2/core·h, which conflicts with the price table. If ¥0.2 is real, the unit price is ¥0.60/h (+36%).

INTERNATIONAL (Singapore), same hours

| DAU | Compute | + Pro | Total/month |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 172.5 × 0.0992 = $17.1 | $149 | $166 |
| 100 | 1,725 × 0.0992 = $171.1 | $149 | $320 |

OTHER COSTS
- Usually zero: Credits are used only by AgentBay's own LLM tools (page_use_act and friends). They cost 16.8 credits per million input tokens = ¥0.84/M and 134.4 per million output tokens = ¥6.72/M; we do not use them.

- Live-view video goes directly between the phone and Wuying, not through our servers. CDP commands from Tokyo are small. I assume screenshots arrive as inbound traffic, which is not charged on a pay-by-traffic EIP (unverified).

options.ux:
- WHILE THE AGENT WORKS: browser steps appear in the conversation as tool-call cards, for example "Opened jd.com" or "Clicked 搜索". No screenshots unless we do the optional thumbnail item. A run with a live browser shows a "Watch" button.

- LIVE VIEW: tapping Watch opens a full-screen in-app WebView with AgentBay's resource_url, which the docs describe as a "real-time video stream and full mouse/keyboard control" of the cloud browser.
  - A watch-only mode may be possible: the &input=true&keyboard=true switches are documented for MCP links, but unverified for resource_url.
  - Links have limited validity and a limited number of opens (exact values unknown), so the app fetches a fresh link each time.
  - The video goes straight between the phone and Wuying (its ASP protocol), not through our servers.

- TAKEOVER FOR LOGINS, CAPTCHAS AND PAYMENTS:
  1. The agent asks, for example "Please log in to Taobao".
  2. The user gets a push and an inbox item: "Your agent needs you in the browser".
  3. The user taps it. The live view opens with control, already on that page's site.
  4. The user logs in on the phone. The password is typed into the cloud browser, so the agent and the model never see it.
  5. The user taps "Done". The agent continues in a follow-up run a few seconds later.
  - While waiting, no browser is running and nothing is billed.
  - Slider CAPTCHAs may be solved automatically (solve_captchas: slider only, "typically within 30 seconds"). Other CAPTCHAs fall back to takeover.

- SAVED LOGINS: each agent instance has its own saved browser data (cookies, localStorage) in an AgentBay context, so the user logs in once.
  - Instance settings show "Browser logins saved · last used …" and a "Forget logins" button.
  - Caveat: every session is a fresh VM, and the IP may change between sessions. Sites with risk control (Taobao, banks, WeChat web) may ask the user to verify again or refuse. Persistent device fingerprints are listed as an Ultra-only feature.
  - With the Hangzhou option, posts show a mainland province as IP location (likely 浙江, inferred). With Singapore they show 新加坡.

- SPEED (nothing measured yet; the spike work item measures it):
  - The first browser step in a run waits for session create + InitBrowser + CDP connect.
  - Each later step goes agent → Tokyo server → Hangzhou (or Singapore) and back, plus model thinking time. Expect it to feel slower than a person.
  - The browser can't hold mid-page state across a takeover: only cookies and storage persist, so the agent re-opens the page afterwards.

- PHONE FIT: the cloud browser renders at a desktop or configurable viewport (up to 1920×1080, or adaptive). Pinch-zoom and Chinese IME input inside the WebView must be tested. Neither app has a WebView today (Android renders Markdown natively, apps/android/README.md:316).

- WHICH AGENTS: Claude, Codex and Hermes get the browser on day one. OpenClaw and Pi get it after the optional MCP-injection item. Unless the plan allows "may browse the web", Claude and Codex would ask for approval on every click.
options.security_compliance:
API KEY
- One platform key per account and region. It controls every session and every saved context, which means all users' cookies. That makes it our most sensitive new secret.
- Where it lives: THINKTIN_AGENTBAY_API_KEY in the k8s Secret for thinktin-worker (tool calls, sweeper) and thinktin-api (live-view links). Loaded in crates/server/src/config.rs with redacted Debug, like aliyun_kms_access_key_secret.
- It never goes to the sandbox, the shim, the apps, events or logs.
- The key travels in the form body (Authorization=Bearer …, verified in SDK api/client.py), so request-body tracing must stay off.
- Responses contain bearer URLs (ResourceUrl, WsUrl, the CDP link) and must be redacted too.
- Rotation: allow two configured keys; keys are created and revoked in the AgentBay console. Unknown: whether keys can be scoped like RAM users. The trial is for real-name main accounts only.

PER-USER ISOLATION
- Vendor side (a claim we cannot audit): each session is its own hardware-virtualized VM with its own kernel and file system, no public IP, isolated from other sessions, and destroyed on release (security whitepaper 2026-10-13).
- Our side: contexts are account-wide objects, so isolation between our users rests entirely on our mapping.
  - Session and context are chosen only from ToolContext (run → instance → user) and a tenant-scoped DB row, never from agent arguments (same rule as orchestrator/src/computer.rs).
  - One context and at most one active session per instance, enforced with a unique partial index. A browser profile cannot be opened twice, and AgentBay does not document concurrent use of one context.
  - Labels and ExternalUserId carry opaque UUIDs only, never phone numbers.
- resource_url handling:
  - Fetched fresh for the owning user's authenticated call only, served no-store and audited.
  - Never put into events, push payloads, IM channels or the agent's view.
- The CDP URL stays in worker memory.

DATA AND DELETION
- Cookies, localStorage and (if enabled) rrweb replays live in AgentBay-managed storage. The domestic product page claims KMS encryption to 国密 standard, but this data is not under our per-user DEK, so our crypto-shred in store::Tx::erase_account does not reach it.
- Required: DeleteContext plus session release on account and instance deletion (an outbox job), recorded in docs/compliance.md section 5.
- Replay off by default (EnableRecord=false), because it records everything the user does on the page.
- Hangzhou: the data stays in mainland China, with Alibaba as an entrusted processor. That needs a processing agreement and disclosure in the privacy policy. Page content and screenshots still flow to Tokyo and to model providers, the cross-border question we already have.
- Singapore: users' cookies are stored abroad, which needs PIPL Art. 38 measures (CAC standard contract etc.) and Art. 39 separate consent.

WEB RISK
- Web pages are untrusted and can carry prompt injection. Tool results go back marked as external data.
- The agent can type anything it knows into any site, including vault values it has revealed. The optional browser_fill_secret tool keeps the secret server-side and bound to one origin.
- Payments and irreversible submits cannot be detected reliably. We combine AgentBay's 103 "pay request", agent instructions and user takeover; there is no technical guarantee.
- The browser's outbound traffic cannot be allowlisted: AgentBay's domain policy is Windows-only, and *.aliyuncs.com is always allowed. Controls are therefore per-user minutes per day, one concurrent session per instance, and a global cap.
- Upside: the browser runs outside our VPC, so it cannot reach our metadata service or internal services (inferred).

TERMS AND LAW
- AgentBay forbids 刷单/刷榜 (order-brushing, ranking manipulation) with fake accounts. Automated collection falls under Art. 18 of the Network Data Security Regulations. Our ToS must pass both on to users.
- The Web SDK terms say "for use by yourself or your enterprise only". We need Alibaba's written OK to show live views to our end users.
- GetLink needs enterprise real-name verification and was whitelist-only in Oct 2025. resource_url may not need it (unverified).
- No AgentBay SLA was found. Its certifications (ISO 27001, SOC, 等保) are Alibaba-wide, not AgentBay-specific.
risks: Plan floor: CDP control needs Pro (¥999/month domestic, $149 international). For 10 test users that is 93% of the browser bill (about ¥1,075/month), more than twice today's whole launch budget of ¥390–450/month.

No Tokyo region (DNS NXDOMAIN, checked 2026-10-29). Every CDP step crosses the border, Tokyo↔Hangzhou, and latency and jitter are unmeasured. A Singapore account is a new account; our earlier international account got stuck at real-name verification.

Egress location is a trade-off with no good answer. Hangzhou cannot reach Google, YouTube, Wikipedia, X or ChatGPT, and GitHub only partly. Singapore shows 新加坡 on Chinese sites and likely triggers Taobao, WeChat and bank risk controls. Covering both means two plans and logins split by region.

Live view on phones is unproven: WebView control, Chinese IME, link validity and open-count limits (values unknown), and whether Alibaba's terms allow showing it to our end users ('yourself or your enterprise only').

call_for_user waits at most 180 s, which is too short for a reply driven by a push notification. We need our own wait-and-follow-up flow, and mid-page state is lost across a takeover (only cookies and storage persist).
Idle sessions keep billing. A worker crash leaks sessions until idle release (minimum 3 minutes) or max runtime. The label sweeper is mandatory, and manual_release must never be used without it.

Vendor maturity. The SDK is pre-1.0 (0.22) and changing: the CDP link moved to a separate GetCdpLink API. Several features are Beta, the docs contradict each other (endpoint, bandwidth, image limits, CPU price in the billing example), no SLA was found, and there is no Rust SDK; we would implement the API by reading the generated Python code.
A leaked platform API key exposes every user's saved browser contexts and lets the holder run sessions on our bill.
Cookies live in Alibaba storage outside our per-user encryption. Missing a DeleteContext on account deletion would leave data behind after we tell the user it is erased.
Concurrency limits: Pro allows 200 sessions. At 1000 DAU × 60 min/day the peak is about 288, so Ultra plus ¥10 per extra session per month.
Agent reach and approvals: only Claude, Codex and Hermes get platform tools today. Without per-tool pre-authorization, Claude and Codex ask on every click.

Anti-bot: datacenter IPs, a fresh VM per session and changing IPs; persistent device fingerprints are Ultra-only. Saved logins may be challenged or blocked by risk-control-heavy sites, and CAPTCHA auto-solving covers sliders only.
Unknowns that move the cost: the browser_latest CPU/RAM spec is unpublished (4c8g would double the price), and the billing example's ¥0.2/core·h would add 36%.
File downloads and uploads from inside the cloud browser are undocumented, so tasks like 'download the invoice PDF' may not work in v1.
The browser's outbound traffic cannot be filtered on our side (Linux allowlist unsupported, *.aliyuncs.com always open), so policy rests on caps, ToS and agent instructions.
strengths: The agent sandbox stays locked to the model gateway. Browsing does not wait for the egress proxy (WBS 2.7), and nothing is added to the 0.5–0.9 GB templates or their 1–2 GiB memory.

Live view and human takeover come ready-made: a real-time stream with mouse and keyboard, the call_for_user protocol (login/captcha/pay), slider CAPTCHA solving, stealth, proxies and replay. These would take weeks to build ourselves.
Each session is a separate hardware VM outside our VPC, so a hijacked browser cannot reach our internal services or the metadata endpoint.

It fits code we already have: a PlatformTools provider modelled on computer_*, follow-up runs modelled on vault_request, routing only from the ToolContext. The CDP URL and API key never leave the server.
No browser cost between runs. Sessions are billed per second and released at run end, and logins survive in a per-instance context.
The Hangzhou option gives a mainland IP, which suits logged-in Chinese sites; the Tokyo deployment cannot offer that.

Easy to switch later: the agent-facing browser_* tools sit on standard CDP, so the backend can move to a self-built Chromium, an FC/ACS browser sandbox, or the user's own computer (WBS 14.4 reuses crates/browser) without changing what agents see.
Per-hour compute is close to ACS (¥0.44/h against ¥0.354/h for an equivalent Tokyo pod add-on), so beyond the plan fee the premium is small.
options.when_best:
Buying is the best choice in these cases:
- We want agents to browse, including on logged-in Chinese sites with phone takeover for logins and CAPTCHAs, before we have built the egress proxy (WBS 2.7) and our own live view.
- We have enough active users to absorb the plan fee. At about 100 DAU it is about ¥10 of the ¥17.6 per user per month.
- A mainland exit IP (Hangzhou, our existing domestic account) is what the users' tasks need.

Buying is not the best choice in these cases:
- The 10-user test stage. The ¥999/month plan alone is more than twice today's whole launch budget.
- Mostly foreign-site research. Hangzhou cannot reach Google, ChatGPT and others; Singapore needs a new international account and brings cross-border consent duties.
- We need strict control of where the browser can go, or of where cookies are stored.

Suggested path:
1. Run the 2-day spike on a trial or one month of Pro. This settles latency, phone live view, saved logins and the real spec.
2. Build the browser_* tools so the backend can be swapped.
3. Launch on AgentBay Hangzhou only if the spike passes and paying users can absorb the plan fee.
4. Otherwise keep the same tools and switch to a self-built Chromium once the egress proxy (WBS 2.7) exists.

options.name: Hybrid, built mostly by us: a browser in each agent's own sandbox that goes out through our Tokyo egress proxy (default); the user's own computer for "act as me" sites (already planned); a rented AgentBay mainland browser added only when demand shows up
options.architecture:
Three tiers. Every tier gives the agents the same browser tools and the same live view.

TIER 1: BUILD NOW (DEFAULT). A browser inside the instance's own sandbox. It reaches the web from Tokyo through our own egress proxy.

1. Image
- Each agent template gets a "-browser" variant (deploy/templates/Dockerfile) that adds:
  - Debian trixie `chromium` 156: 324 MB installed (packages.debian.org).
  - `fonts-noto-cjk`: 91 MB installed (packages.debian.org/trixie/fonts-noto-cjk, checked 2026-10-29).
  - A pinned `@playwright/mcp` 0.0.83 (Apache-2.0).
- The Claude template grows from 695 MB to about 1.1 GB.
- On ACS, each variant is its own SandboxSet (deploy/aliyun/acs.py), with a preheat pool of 0.
- Planned size is 2 vCPU / 4 GiB [A]. Drop to 1 vCPU / 3 GiB if the Phase 0 measurement allows. Idle headless Chromium alone peaks around 700 MB. Nobody has measured it inside our sandbox.
- Only instances where the user turns the browser on use the variant. The choice takes effect at the next sandbox (re)create, through the existing archive and restore.

2. Process
- agent-shim starts Chromium as a sidecar, using the same mechanism as the OpenClaw gateway sidecar.
- Flags: `--headless=new --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir=$HOME/.browser --proxy-server=http://127.0.0.1:3128 --no-sandbox --disable-dev-shm-usage --disable-quic --lang=zh-CN`.
- `--no-sandbox` is there because user namespaces are probably not available as uid 1001. The ACS MicroVM pod is the isolation boundary.
- CDP listens on loopback only.
- After an archive restore, the shim deletes stale Singleton* lock files before starting. Otherwise Chromium would refuse a profile last used "on another computer".

3. Tools: one browser surface for all five agents
- The browser server is Playwright MCP with `--cdp-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9222`. It offers accessibility snapshots, click and type by element ref, screenshots, and file upload. Downloads land in the workspace and can be saved with the existing artifact tools.
- Claude, Codex and Hermes receive it through per-session ACP mcpServers, next to the existing `thinktin` bridge (agent-shim acp.rs / claude_cli.rs).
- OpenClaw and Pi ignore per-session MCP. For them, config.rs writes the server into openclaw.json `mcp.servers` and `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json`. The same change gives these two agents our platform tools for the first time.
- OpenClaw's native browser plugin is turned off.
- Hermes's native browser stays hidden, because agent-browser is not installed.
- Vendor browsers are not possible here. Claude in Chrome is off under token auth. Codex Browser exists only in the ChatGPT desktop app.

4. Egress (WBS 2.7, built as part of this project)
- A new proxy, `crates/egress`, runs on the Tokyo service machine on port 3128. Only the sandbox vSwitch can reach it.
  - Sandbox allowOut already lists that machine's IP, and allowOut has no ports, so the only network change is one security-group rule.
- It handles HTTP CONNECT without TLS interception, plus plain HTTP.
- Authentication:
  - The shim's local forwarder on 127.0.0.1:3128 adds Proxy-Authorization with the sandbox's current token.
  - The proxy checks that token the way llm-gw does: signature, Pod-IP binding, current sandbox, grant.
  - Chromium cannot put credentials in `--proxy-server`, which is why the local forwarder is needed.
- Policy:
  - DNS is resolved inside the proxy, and connections go only to public addresses (reusing the `llm_gw::ssrf` rules).
  - Blocked: 100.100.100.200 metadata, RFC1918, our VPC CIDRs, CGNAT, loopback, link-local and ULA.
  - Ports 80 and 443 only.
  - Per-instance caps on bandwidth and connections, plus a daily byte quota.
  - An optional domain denylist, for example payment sites.
  - A per-template mode: model-only or web.
- Logging: instance, host, bytes and time for each connection. No URLs and no content.
- The same proxy gives agents' curl, pip and npm controlled internet access through HTTPS_PROXY whenever web mode is on.
- Because inbound EIP traffic is not billed, the web data itself costs almost nothing.

5. Persistence
- The browser profile lives under the agent HOME (workspace/.thinktin/home/.browser).
- Cookies and logins therefore travel in the existing workspace archive, encrypted with the user's DEK (AES-256-GCM) and stored in OSS in Tokyo.
- Caches are excluded (Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache, CacheStorage) in crates/control/src/workspace.rs. The profile is capped at about 300 MB [A], to stay well under the 4 GiB archive cap.
- The browser process does not survive pause or archive. The logins do.

6. Live view and user takeover
- No new sandbox port and no SandboxProvider change.
- While someone is watching, the shim connects as a second CDP client and runs Page.startScreencast (720 px JPEG, fps capped).
- Frames go up the shim's existing stdout JSON-lines channel as a new ShimEvent::BrowserFrame.
- The orchestrator puts them on an in-memory broadcast per instance. They are never written to the run log, which cuts strings at 16 KiB.
- A new owner-only gateway WebSocket, /v1/instances/{id}/browser/live, sends them to the app.
- Input goes back the same way (ShimCommand::BrowserInput, then CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent / dispatchKeyEvent / insertText):
  - taps;
  - committed text, so phone Chinese input methods work;
  - keys;
  - scrolls.
- Keystrokes are never logged.
- The server is a single node today. Several nodes would need routing from the gateway node to the executor's node.

7. Approvals
- `browser` becomes a run-grant capability.
- When it is granted, the shim pre-approves the browser MCP tools in Claude's settings and in Codex's `[mcp_servers]` approval mode. Otherwise the phone would be asked on every click. Hermes does not ask.
- A new platform tool, `browser_takeover(reason)`:
  - puts the run into waiting_approval with wait code `browser_takeover`;
  - pushes an inbox card ("需要你登录 xx", i.e. "please log in to xx");
  - returns when the user taps 完成 (done) or 放弃 (give up);
  - has its own timeout of 30 minutes [A], after which the sandbox may pause. The Tokyo config keeps the sandbox running during approval waits, and without this cap an abandoned takeover would burn ¥0.49/h for up to 24 h.
- Optional `browser_fill_secret(vault name)`: the shim types a vault password into the focused field over CDP, so the model never sees it.

TIER 2: ALREADY PLANNED, NO NEW WORK HERE. The user's own computer for "act as me" on personal logged-in sites (bank, Taobao, WeChat).
- Uses the existing computer_open / screenshot / click tools over the desktop app and relay.
- It has the user's real IP, device and cookies.
- It is Mac-only and has never run on a real Mac.
- When WBS 14.4 adds CDP control, it must use a dedicated automation Chrome profile, because Chrome 136+ ignores remote debugging on the default profile.

TIER 3: ONLY WHEN DEMAND APPEARS. A mainland-IP cloud browser rented from AgentBay on our existing domestic account. The domestic key only works in mainland regions, which is exactly what this tier needs.
- The server holds the API key. The key never enters the sandbox.
- It creates a browser_latest session with one BrowserContext per instance (cookies persist on the AgentBay side) and gets its CDP URL (GetCdpLink, which needs the Pro plan).
- It hands that URL to the shim. The shim forwards 127.0.0.1:9223 to it through our egress proxy, and a second Playwright MCP (tools named browser_cn_*) attaches there.
- Our own screencast code works over that CDP, so live view needs neither GetLink (needs enterprise verification, was whitelist-only) nor the Web SDK (its terms say "for your own enterprise only").
- Sessions are released with sync_context after 3–5 minutes idle, because idle sessions are billed.

NOT CHOSEN, AND WHY
- FC AgentRun / Cloud Sandbox: invite-only preview, no region list published, a separate sandbox per agent, and its VNC needs a header-injecting proxy.
- International SaaS (Browserbase, Steel and others): hosted in the US or EU, triggers PIPL Articles 38/39, and gains nothing over Tokyo.
- Browserless: SSPL licence.
- A shared ACS browser-pool service: sandboxes are deliberately isolated from each other, and profile persistence would become a second system. It is only worth it if Phase 0 forces 2C/4G and usage passes about 500 DAU (see cost model).

options.cost_model:
PRICES USED
- ACS Agent Sandbox, overseas rate (covers Tokyo): ¥0.1232 per vCPU-hour, ¥0.0616 per GiB-hour.
  - Source: help.aliyun.com/zh/cs/user-guide/agent-sandbox/.
  - It matches docs/deploy-aliyun-sg.md: ¥0.123 / ¥0.062, and "1C2G ≈ ¥0.25/h".
- Tokyo EIP, pay by traffic: BGP ¥0.60/GB, BGP 精品 ¥3.0/GB. Inbound traffic is not billed.
  - Source: help.aliyun.com/zh/eip/pay-as-you-go/, checked 2026-10-29.
- ecs.e-c1m2.large: ¥117.67/month (docs/deploy-aliyun-sg.md section 8.9).
- AgentBay, domestic site: Pro ¥999/month; CPU ¥0.12 per core-hour; memory ¥0.05 per GB-hour; billed per second; idle sessions billed. Source: AgentBay billing page, 2026-06-24.
- AgentBay, international site: Pro $149/month; $0.027 per core-hour; $0.0113 per GB-hour.

ASSUMPTIONS [A]
- A1: each DAU has 1 sandbox-running hour per day (the docs 8.9 planning figure); 30 days a month.
- A2: 20 browser-minutes per DAU per day. Heavy case: 60.
- A3: every DAU has the browser turned on. This is an upper bound; cost scales linearly with the share that actually does.
- A4: the browser variant adds 1 vCPU and 2 GiB (2C/4G). A lean variant adds only 1 GiB (1C/3G). Neither is measured. Codex and Pi start from 1 GiB, so their 2C/4G step adds 1 vCPU and 3 GiB: ¥0.308/h, or ¥9.24 per DAU-month.
- A5: 3 MB of page data per browser-minute; outbound request bytes are 10% of that.
- A6: live view is watched 5 minutes per DAU per day at about 120 KB/s (720 px JPEG, ~40 KB × 3 fps).
- A7: AgentBay browser_latest is 2c4g. Its real spec is unpublished; 2c4g is the custom-image default.
- A8: AgentBay adds 3 minutes of idle tail per session (the backend minimum), with 2 sessions per day.
- A9: browsing is spread over 8 busy hours, with 3× bursts.

TIER 1, SELF-BUILT, PER DAU PER MONTH
- Compute, 2C/4G: (0.1232 + 2 × 0.0616) = ¥0.2464/h × 30 h = ¥7.39.
- Compute, lean 1C/3G: 0.0616 × 30 = ¥1.85.
- Web traffic: 20 min × 3 MB × 30 = 1.8 GB inbound, which is free. Outbound is 0.18 GB × 0.6 = ¥0.11 (¥0.54 on 精品).
- Live view: 5 × 60 s × 120 KB = 36 MB/day, or 1.08 GB/month × 0.6 = ¥0.65 (¥3.24 on 精品).
- Proxy host:
  - At 100 DAU it runs on the existing service machine for ¥0 [A: needs headroom]. Load: 100 × 20 / 480 × 3 ≈ 12 burst browsers, about 5 Mbps.
  - At 1000 DAU: about 125 burst browsers and about 50 Mbps, so two ecs.e-c1m2.large for high availability: ¥235/month.

TIER 1 TOTALS PER MONTH
- 10 test users: 10 × 7.39 = ¥74 (lean ¥18), plus about ¥8 of traffic.
- 100 DAU, 2C/4G: 739 + 11 + 65 + 0 = ¥815 (≈ ¥8.2 per DAU). Lean: 185 + 11 + 65 = ¥261.
- 1000 DAU, 2C/4G: 7,392 + 110 + 650 + 235 = ¥8,387. Lean: 1,848 + 110 + 650 + 235 = ¥2,843.
- Tier 1 compute follows sandbox hours, not browser minutes. Heavy browsing only costs more if it keeps sandboxes running longer.

TIER 3, AGENTBAY DOMESTIC (MAINLAND IP)
Assumption: 20% of DAU use it, 10 min a day plus a 3-minute tail = 13 min/day = 6.5 h/month.
- 2c4g = 2 × 0.12 + 4 × 0.05 = ¥0.44/h, so ¥2.86 per user per month.
- 100 DAU: 20 × 2.86 = 57 + 999 = ¥1,056/month.
- 1000 DAU: 200 × 2.86 = 572 + 999 = ¥1,571/month.
- Peak concurrency is about 200 × 13 / 480 × 3 ≈ 16, well inside Pro's 200.

TIER 2, THE USER'S COMPUTER
- ¥0 of cloud compute. Relay traffic is small.

HYBRID TOTALS PER MONTH (Tier 1 at 2C/4G, plus Tier 3)
- 100 DAU: ¥1,871. Lean: ¥1,317.
- 1000 DAU: ¥9,958 (≈ ¥10 per DAU). Lean: ¥4,414.
- Before Tier 3 is switched on: ¥815 (100 DAU) and ¥8,387 (1000 DAU).

COMPARISONS
- Everything on AgentBay domestic. Each DAU uses 26 min/day (20 + 6 tail) = 13 h/month × 0.44 = ¥5.72.
  - 100 DAU: 572 + 999 = ¥1,571, plus ¥65 for our live view.
  - 1000 DAU: 5,720 + 999 = ¥6,719, plus ¥650.
  - Heavy case (60 + 6 min/day): 33 h × 0.44 = ¥14.52 per DAU, so more than ¥15,500 at 1000 DAU.
  - Against Tier 1 at 2C/4G, AgentBay breaks even at 999 / (7.39 − 5.72) ≈ 600 DAU. That is not a like-for-like comparison, because AgentBay's IP is mainland-only (no Google, GitHub or ChatGPT). Against the lean variant, self-built is always cheaper.
- Everything on AgentBay international (Singapore): 2 × 0.027 + 4 × 0.0113 = $0.0992/h × 13 h = $1.29 per DAU.
  - 100 DAU: $129 + $149 = $278.
  - 1000 DAU: $1,290 + $149 = $1,439.
- Shared ACS browser pool (1C/2G pods only while browsing, 26 min/day including tail): 0.2464 × 13 = ¥3.20 per DAU.
  - 1000 DAU: ¥3,203. That saves about ¥4.2k/month against the 2C/4G variant, but costs more than the lean variant (¥1,848). Decide only after Phase 0.

LEFT OUT
- LLM tokens: they are billed to users' own keys, and browsing is token-heavy.
- OSS storage for profiles: about 100 MB per instance [A], unpriced.
- Engineering: Phases 0+1 are about 56.5 person-days. Stage A (public web, no live view) is about 34.5, of which 11.5 is WBS 2.7 egress needed before launch anyway. Stage B (live view, takeover, vault fill) is about 22. Phase 2 is about 10.
options.ux:
INSTANCE SETTING
- Each instance gets a toggle "让它用浏览器" ("let it use a browser"). It is off by default.
- The toggle carries a note: sites will see a Japan IP, and logins stay with this agent.
- The change applies the next time the sandbox is rebuilt.

DURING A RUN
- Browser steps appear as normal tool steps, for example "打开 example.com" (open) or "点击 登录" (click 'log in').
- Screenshots the agent takes can be saved as artifacts.

LIVE VIEW
- A running run has a "看浏览器" (watch the browser) button. It opens a full-screen view of the agent's current tab.
- The view is JPEG frames: 2–5 fps when the page changes, about 0.3–1 s behind [A].
- It is view-only by default. There is no VNC app and no second login.

TAKEOVER
- "接管" (take over) switches the view to input mode:
  - a tap clicks at that point;
  - a text bar uses the phone's own keyboard (Chinese input works because finished text is sent);
  - a key row offers 回车 / 退格 / Tab / 返回 (Enter / Backspace / Tab / Back);
  - dragging scrolls.
- "完成" (done) hands control back to the agent.
- When the agent reaches a login, a CAPTCHA, a payment or a post, it calls browser_takeover:
  - the user gets a push, "需要你登录 xx" ("please log in to xx"), and a card;
  - the card opens straight into takeover mode;
  - the run waits up to 30 minutes with the sandbox kept running.
- Passwords saved in the vault can be filled in without the model ever seeing them.

SAVED LOGINS
- Cookies and local storage persist for each instance across wakes and archives, encrypted inside the workspace archive.
- They are not shared between instances or with the phone's own browser.
- "清除浏览器登录" (clear browser logins) wipes them.

SPEED
- A single browser action takes about 0.2–2 s on 2 vCPU [A]. Model thinking dominates at 3–10 s per step [A], so a 10-step task takes about 1–2 minutes [A].
- Chinese sites load more slowly from Tokyo than from the mainland.
- The first browser use after a rebuild adds Chromium start-up (about 2–5 s [A]) plus a cold start of the bigger image (not measured).

LIMITS USERS WILL NOTICE
- Sites see a Japan datacenter IP:
  - Xiaohongshu, Weibo and Douyin label posts "日本".
  - Taobao, WeChat and banks may challenge or block the login.
  - Google may show CAPTCHAs on our shared IP.
- For those sites the app suggests "用我的电脑" (use my computer; Tier 2: Mac only, the Mac menubar shows that it is being controlled, and the phone sees one screenshot per step). Later it can suggest the "大陆浏览器" (mainland browser; Tier 3: same tools and the same live view, labelled, with a daily minutes cap).
- There is nothing to watch once the sandbox has paused, which happens after 10 minutes idle.
options.security_compliance:
WHAT STAYS THE SAME
- Isolation does not change. One instance gets one sandbox and one browser. Profiles are never shared, and CDP listens only on loopback.

THE EGRESS PROXY IS THE SECURITY BOUNDARY
- The browser's own filters are explicitly not boundaries: Playwright --allowed-origins, OpenClaw ssrfPolicy, and the agent's self-reported ACP tool kinds.
- The proxy enforces:
  - token-authenticated access, tied to the Pod IP;
  - connections only to public IPs after its own DNS resolution;
  - explicit denies for 100.100.100.200 metadata, our VPC (which contains RDS and sandbox-manager, the latter on plaintext HTTP), RFC1918, CGNAT, loopback, link-local and ULA;
  - ports 80 and 443 only;
  - caps per instance;
  - logs of host and bytes for each instance.
- Chromium runs with --disable-quic. UDP has no route anyway, because there is no NAT.
- This also closes the threat model's top pre-launch item (WBS 2.7).

PROMPT INJECTION AND LOGGED-IN COOKIES
- Web pages are untrusted input, so an injected agent could post or buy using the logged-in cookies.
- Mitigations:
  - the browser is off by default, per instance;
  - the agent is told to call browser_takeover for logins, payments and posts (this is guidance, not a boundary);
  - an optional proxy denylist for payment domains;
  - no logins by default.
- Users must be told plainly that anything they log into in the agent's browser, including passwords typed during takeover, is visible to that agent's sandbox.
- Vault fill keeps passwords out of the model context and out of the logs.

CHROMIUM RUNS WITH --no-sandbox
- A compromised renderer becomes the sandbox user, which holds the sandbox token, the cookies and the workspace.
- That is contained by the MicroVM pod and the proxy.
- Chromium must be patched by rebuilding the template on a fixed schedule, and versions pinned.

DATA AND PRIVACY
- Cookies and profiles are stored in Tokyo:
  - encrypted at rest in OSS with the per-user DEK;
  - crypto-shredded when the account is deleted;
  - while the sandbox is running or paused, they sit on ACS ephemeral storage, whose encryption at rest is not documented.
- The privacy policy needs a line saying browser login state is stored in Tokyo.
- This extends the cross-border transfer (PIPL Articles 38/39) we already have for workspaces. It does not create a new one.
- Keystrokes and frames are never stored. Only the start and end of a takeover are audited.

LEGAL REVIEW NEEDED
- A Tokyo browser that mainland users can watch live and that can open Google, YouTube or X may be read as a circumvention service. Relevant: the MIIT 2017 notice, and Alibaba's terms, which forbid illegal proxies.
- Decide with counsel whether the live view, or certain domains, need restricting.
- Network Data Security Regulations Article 18 (automated collection): the terms of service must forbid scraping, 刷单 (fake orders) and 刷榜 (ranking manipulation), and the proxy's per-instance rate caps back this up.
- Do not market CAPTCHA bypassing.
- How long egress logs must be kept needs legal confirmation [A].
- No ICP filing is needed, because nothing is hosted in the mainland for Tiers 1 and 2.

TIER 3 (AGENTBAY)
- Data stays in the mainland on Alibaba's side: cookies sit in a BrowserContext in Alibaba-managed storage, and replays only if enabled.
- The API key stays on our server.
- We avoid the Web SDK ("for your own enterprise only") and GetLink by using our own screencast over CDP.
- AgentBay's acceptable-use terms forbid 刷单 and 刷榜.

LICENCES
- Fine to use:
  - Chromium (BSD-style plus third-party licences);
  - Playwright and Playwright MCP (Apache-2.0);
  - Noto CJK fonts (OFL).
- Add all of these to tools/licenses/policy.toml.
- Avoid:
  - Browserless (SSPL);
  - nodriver and Lightpanda (AGPL);
  - chrome-devtools-mcp, which turns on telemetry and CrUX lookups by default.
risks: Sizing has not been measured. If Chromium needs 2C/4G, Tier 1 costs about ¥7.4 per DAU per month (¥9.2 for Codex and Pi) instead of about ¥1.9. At 1000 DAU that is roughly ¥8.4k instead of ¥2.8k a month, and the ACS browser pool or AgentBay starts to look competitive.

The egress proxy is new security-critical code that sits next to our VPC. A bug in the DNS or IP checks becomes SSRF into the service machine, RDS or the plaintext sandbox-manager. It needs explicit VPC CIDR denies, tests and fuzzing, and at scale its own host.
Prompt injection plus saved logins can make the agent post, buy or message as the user. Kind-based approvals are not a boundary, and pre-approving browser tools removes the per-click check.

The shared Tokyo datacenter IP: Chinese sites label posts 日本 (Japan) and may block or challenge logins; Google CAPTCHAs are likely; one abusive user can get the IP flagged for everyone. Spreading traffic over several EIPs costs money and is not planned.
Legal: live-viewing blocked foreign sites from Tokyo for mainland users may be treated as a circumvention service. This needs counsel before launch and could force live-view or domain restrictions.

OpenClaw and Pi MCP through their config files is unverified (pi-acp does not wire MCP through, and Pi's mcp.json under rpc mode is undocumented). Tier 1 may first reach only Claude, Codex and Hermes.
Codex's MCP approval-mode semantics and Claude's allow-list syntax for a second MCP server are unverified. If pre-approval fails, every click prompts the phone and the feature is unusable.

Live view rides the shim's stdout through envd and the sandbox-gateway. Throughput, head-of-line blocking with run events, and the 600 s idle timeout are untested. The in-process broadcast assumes a single server node.

CDP Page.startScreencast and Input.insertText are experimental, and the Debian Chromium version moves. We must pin versions and rebuild templates regularly, both for security patches (we run --no-sandbox) and to avoid breakage.
Archive edge cases: stale Singleton* locks; a cookie DB caught mid-write when it is archived (tar can capture files that are changing); caches bloating archives toward the 4 GiB cap.
Takeover waits keep the sandbox running (about ¥0.49/h at 2C/4G). Without the 30-minute cap, an abandoned takeover costs up to about ¥11.8 over the 24 h approval timeout.

Tier 3 AgentBay maturity: Beta labels, contradictory docs, no product SLA, a ¥999/month floor for CDP that could change, unknown Tokyo-to-Hangzhou CDP latency, and a mainland IP that cannot reach Google, GitHub or ChatGPT.
Tier 2 is Mac-only and has never run on a real Mac. Windows users have no 'act as me' path except Tier 3.
Browsing is token-heavy (accessibility snapshots are large). Users' own model bills grow, and complaints may land on us.
strengths: Cheapest at our scale: about ¥74/month extra for the 10 test users, against a ¥999/month floor just to get CDP on AgentBay. At 100 DAU it is ¥261–815/month, against about ¥1,571 for an all-AgentBay design.
Most of the hardest piece (the egress proxy, WBS 2.7) is pre-launch security work we must do anyway. The browser reuses it instead of adding a second network path.
It keeps the existing isolation model: one instance, one sandbox, one browser, with outbound traffic only through our policy. No new vendor, account or region for the default path.
Logins persist for free in the already-encrypted workspace archive (per-user DEK, crypto-shred on account deletion).
One tool surface (Playwright MCP over CDP) for all five agents, with one policy. Tier 3 swaps only the CDP endpoint, so agents and the live view do not change.
Live view and takeover use our own app and gateway, so we are not tied to vendor viewer links that need enterprise verification and allow only limited opens, or to Web SDK terms.
Side benefit: writing MCP config for OpenClaw and Pi gives those two agents our platform tools (schedule, artifact, computer) for the first time.

Each limitation has a fallback rather than a dead end: Japan IP leads to the user's Mac (Tier 2) or the mainland browser (Tier 3); CAPTCHAs and logins lead to takeover; heavy cost leads to the lean size or a browser pool after measurement.
